title: India says Hasina's return is separate from extradition as Dhaka deploys 108 border guard platoons
dek: Delhi drew a line between the ousted leader's plan to fly home on 16 December and Bangladesh's extradition request. Dhaka insists she can return only in custody and has sent troops into seven districts ahead of an Awami League lockdown.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
India said on Wednesday that Sheikh Hasina's plan to return to Bangladesh and Dhaka's request for her extradition are two separate matters, its clearest statement yet since the ousted Bangladeshi prime minister named 16 December as the date she would fly home from exile in Delhi. "The case of a citizen willing to return voluntarily to her country on a travel document is a matter separate from the extradition request," Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said at the ministry's briefing, adding that her return was a matter "between the former Prime Minister and the Bangladesh government".

Bangladesh, which says she can come back only through extradition, has meanwhile stepped up security. The Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) said on Wednesday it had deployed 108 platoons in seven districts, 56 of them in Hasina's home district of Gopalganj, as the banned Awami League promotes a nationwide "lockdown" for 29 and 30 November.

## India's position

Mr Jaiswal said Bangladesh's extradition request, made under the interim government led by Muhammad Yunus, was "being examined in line with our established processes". Earlier this month Hasina asked Bangladesh's High Commission, through a UK-based law firm, to issue her a fresh passport so that she could travel home, according to reports.

The spokesperson also voiced concern about law and order in Bangladesh. "We understandably are concerned at the incidents of violence against minorities in Bangladesh. We urge the government of Bangladesh to thoroughly investigate these incidents and bring the perpetrators to justice," he said.

Dhaka's position has not moved. Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said on Wednesday that "a convicted fugitive" could return only through the extradition process, that the government felt "no worry or pressure" over her shifting deadlines, and that the Awami League would face strict legal action if it resorted to militancy, arson or attacks on people and property, according to reports.

## How the dispute began

On Tuesday, 24 November, Hasina's spokesperson said she planned to fly home on 16 December, Victory Day, and asked the Bangladeshi government to arrange her flight on the state carrier, Biman Bangladesh Airlines. It was the first time she had named a date since she fled Dhaka for Delhi on 5 August 2024.

Dhaka rejected the request within hours. "She is not a regular commercial passenger," Humaiun Kobir, a state minister for foreign affairs, told reporters at the foreign ministry that morning. "She will have to return only in handcuffs or under strict surveillance." The government says she can come back only through extradition from India, where she has lived for more than two years. That puts the decision, and the pressure, on New Delhi.

## What happened

Hasina's spokesperson, Syed Mozammel Ali, said she "now calls upon the government to arrange for her air transport from Delhi back to Dhaka", noting that she had been flown to India on a Bangladeshi aircraft in August 2024. "It is deeply symbolic that she has chosen 16 December, our Victory Day," he said in a statement. The date marks the end of the 1971 Liberation War, which her father, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, led. An aide, Abu Obaidha Arin, said: "We firmly believe that she will celebrate this historic day among her people." Earlier this month Hasina said in an interview that she would return in December "at any cost". Her claims could not be independently verified.

Mr Kobir called her "a convicted criminal; a fugitive terrorist" and said Bangladesh "will not entertain any such delusional request", according to reports. "No terrorist will ever be allowed to return this way without extradition," he told reporters. Asked about a recent string of violent attacks, he blamed what he called "Awami terrorism, sponsored by Hasina from Delhi".

Abu Abdullah M Saleh, press secretary to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, said in an interview: "My government's stand is very clear. She has been convicted in a tribunal." The government has sought her extradition, he said. An unnamed minister said on 22 November that Hasina would be arrested and jailed on arrival, and that there had been no official talks with India about an aircraft, according to reports.

## Troops on the streets

The BGB's new deployment, announced in a press statement on Wednesday, is larger and more concentrated than the one it announced a day earlier. Of the 108 platoons, 56 are in Gopalganj, 18 in Dhaka, 18 in Gazipur, six in Narayanganj, three in Chattogram, two in Mymensingh and one in Cox's Bazar, with four more on standby, the BGB said, according to reports. A platoon has 30 to 40 personnel. The deployment, on the home ministry's instructions, is "to maintain law and order, ensure public safety and deal with any untoward situation", it said. About 2,000 police and 10 BGB platoons had already been sent to Gopalganj last week, according to reports.

Arson attacks on trains, buses and banks have been reported across Bangladesh in recent days, and police have blamed activists of the Awami League and its affiliates for several of them, according to reports. In Gopalganj on 23 November, at least 30 people were injured in two clashes linked to processions by the Awami League and its affiliates, whose activities are banned. Four crude bombs went off and at least 12 shops were vandalised, according to reports from the district. The Awami League's call for a lockdown on 29 and 30 November has been circulated through online platforms.

## Background

Hasina ruled Bangladesh for 15 years until a student-led uprising forced her out in August 2024. The UN human rights office has said as many as 1,400 people may have been killed during the unrest. In November 2025 the International Crimes Tribunal in Dhaka sentenced her to death in absentia for crimes against humanity over the crackdown. She rejects the verdict and denies the charges, and a prosecutor has said she missed the deadline to appeal. Bangladesh allows presidential clemency, but she has not sought it.

The interim government led by Muhammad Yunus banned the Awami League's activities, and the party was barred from the February 2026 election. The Bangladesh Nationalist Party won it, and Tarique Rahman became prime minister. Jamaat-e-Islami is now the main opposition. Violence has risen since Hasina sought a new passport and other documents earlier this month, according to reports.

India has not said whether it will hand her over. In April the MEA said it was examining the extradition request and wanted to "engage constructively with the new government", and on Wednesday it repeated that the request was being examined.

## Why it matters for India and Bengal

Whatever Hasina does on 16 December, India is in the middle. Allowing her to fly to Dhaka would look to Bangladesh's government like India letting a convicted fugitive stage a political return; stopping her, or keeping her indefinitely, keeps the extradition dispute alive at a time when Delhi has said repeatedly that it wants a constructive relationship with the new government in Dhaka.

The dispute also lands on West Bengal's doorstep. On 22 November four senior Awami League leaders living in India visited the Petrapole land port in North 24 Parganas, Bangladesh's busiest trade crossing with India, and at the tribunal in Dhaka on 24 November reporters asked whether the government had failed by letting fugitives reach border areas such as Petrapole and Agartala. Any unrest around 16 December could affect the 2,217-km Bengal stretch of the border, cross-border trade and the movement of people.

It comes as other files between the two countries are open. The 1996 Ganges Water Treaty, which governs how the river's dry-season flow at Farakka is shared, expires on 12 December, and no date has been set for renewal talks.

## What happens next

- 29-30 November: the Awami League's called "lockdown" across Bangladesh.
- 12 December: the Ganges Water Treaty expires.
- 16 December: Hasina's stated return date, Victory Day in Bangladesh.

Whether Hasina can travel at all depends on documents Dhaka has so far refused to issue; India has now said publicly that this is a matter for her and the Bangladeshi government.
